title: Differentiation and integration
summary: For $C^1$ functions, $\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a)$; derivatives obey the product and chain rules.
body:
For $C^1$ functions, $\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a)$; derivatives obey the product and chain rules.

Use integration by parts for absolutely continuous factors. Interchange a derivative and an integral when an integrable bound dominates the differentiated integrand locally; interchange mixed partial derivatives when they are continuous.

title: Dirac delta
summary: The point distribution at $\mathbf a$ evaluates a smooth test function: $\int\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\phi(\mathbf r)\,d^3r=\phi(\mathbf a)$.
body:
The point distribution at $\mathbf a$ evaluates a smooth test function: $\int\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\phi(\mathbf r)\,d^3r=\phi(\mathbf a)$.

The integral denotes distributional pairing with a compactly supported smooth function.

title: Local inverse theorem
summary: A $C^1$ map with $\det DF(x_0)\ne0$ has a differentiable inverse near $x_0$.
body:
A $C^1$ map with $\det DF(x_0)\ne0$ has a differentiable inverse near $x_0$.

Parameters held fixed during inversion can be restored as smooth arguments when the parameter-dependent map is smooth.

title: Localized test functions
summary: Every open interval contains a nonnegative $\eta\in C_c^\infty$ with $\int\eta\,dt>0$.
body:
Every open interval contains a nonnegative $\eta\in C_c^\infty$ with $\int\eta\,dt>0$.

For an interval containing $[a-r,a+r]$, take $\eta(t)=\exp[-1/(1-((t-a)/r)^2)]$ for $|t-a|<r$ and zero elsewhere.

Repeated indices are summed. The scalar Laplacian is $

title: Divergence and Stokes theorems
summary: For $C^1$ fields, $\int_\Omega\nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV=\oint_{\partial\Omega}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf a$ and $\int_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf a=\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$.
body:
For $C^1$ fields, $\int_\Omega\nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV=\oint_{\partial\Omega}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf a$ and $\int_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf a=\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$.

Use the outward normal for a volume and the induced right-hand boundary orientation for a surface.
assumptions: Piecewise smooth oriented regions, with the field continuously differentiable up to each patch boundary.
proof:
On a regular volume chart $\mathbf r(u,v,w)$ with positive Jacobian $J$, write the cyclic flux densities on coordinate faces.
$$G_u=\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot(\mathbf r_v\times\mathbf r_w),\qquad J=\mathbf r_u\cdot(\mathbf r_v\times\mathbf r_w).$$
In the cyclic sum of derivatives the mixed derivatives of the chart cancel in pairs; the cofactor identity contracts the derivative of the field to its trace.
$$\partial_uG_u+\partial_vG_v+\partial_wG_w=J\,\partial_iF_i.$$
Integrating over a parameter box gives its six outward face fluxes by the fundamental theorem. Subdivide into oriented charts; internal fluxes cancel and the boundary faces give the volume formula. Piecewise smooth boundaries follow by subdivision and limits.
On a surface patch pull the line integral back to parameter space.
$$P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf r_u,\qquad Q=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf r_v,\qquad \partial_uQ-\partial_vP=(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v).$$
Apply the fundamental theorem to the two parameter derivatives on a rectangle.
$$\int(\partial_uQ-\partial_vP)\,du\,dv=\oint(P\,du+Q\,dv).$$
Adjacent patches traverse shared edges in opposite directions, leaving the circulation along the external boundary.

integrates the derivative in each coordinate

title: Complex Hilbert space
summary: A Hilbert space is a complex inner-product space complete in $\|\psi\|=\sqrt{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle}$.
body:
A Hilbert space is a complex inner-product space complete in $\|\psi\|=\sqrt{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle}$.

The product is linear in the ket. In $L^2(I)$, $\langle\phi|\psi\rangle=\int_I\phi^*\psi\,dx$; functions equal almost everywhere represent the same vector.

title: Sine and cosine bases
summary: On $(0,L)$, $\{\sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)\}_{n\ge1}$ and $\{1/\sqrt L\}\cup\{\sqrt{2/L}\cos(n\pi x/L)\}_{n\ge1}$ are each complete orthonormal bases of $L^2(0,L)$.
body:
On $(0,L)$, $\{\sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)\}_{n\ge1}$ and $\{1/\sqrt L\}\cup\{\sqrt{2/L}\cos(n\pi x/L)\}_{n\ge1}$ are each complete orthonormal bases of $L^2(0,L)$.

Completeness means convergence in the $L^2$ norm. The cosine family includes the constant mode. Pointwise or endpoint convergence requires separate conditions.

relations.basis: specifies the norm and inner product

title: Parseval identity
summary: For a complete orthonormal basis $(e_n)$ and $f$ in its Hilbert space, $\sum_n|\langle e_n|f\rangle|^2=\|f\|^2$.
body:
For a complete orthonormal basis $(e_n)$ and $f$ in its Hilbert space, $\sum_n|\langle e_n|f\rangle|^2=\|f\|^2$.

The basis may be real or complex; the expansion converges in norm.
proof:
Project onto the span of the first basis vectors.
$$c_n=\langle e_n|f\rangle,\qquad P_Nf=\sum_{n=1}^Nc_ne_n,\qquad \langle e_j|f-P_Nf\rangle=0\quad(j\le N).$$
Orthogonality removes the cross term in the squared norm.
$$\|f\|^2=\|f-P_Nf\|^2+\sum_{n=1}^N|c_n|^2.$$
Completeness gives convergence of these projections in norm, so the remainder tends to zero.

relations.basis: defines the norm and orthogonality

title: Finite-interval Parseval identity
summary: For $f\in L^2(0,L)$, its normalized sine coefficients $s_n$ and cosine coefficients $c_n$ obey $\int_0^L |f|^2\,dx=\sum_{n\ge1}|s_n|^2=\sum_{n\ge0}|c_n|^2$.
body:
For $f\in L^2(0,L)$, its normalized sine coefficients $s_n$ and cosine coefficients $c_n$ obey $\int_0^L |f|^2\,dx=\sum_{n\ge1}|s_n|^2=\sum_{n\ge0}|c_n|^2$.

Take coefficients against each normalized basis on an interval of length $L>0$.
proof:
Use the real normalized modes in the Hilbert inner product to obtain the coefficients.
$$s_n=\sqrt{2/L}\int_0^L f(x)\sin(n\pi x/L)\,dx,\qquad c_n=\sqrt{2/L}\int_0^L f(x)\cos(n\pi x/L)\,dx\quad(n\ge1).$$
The constant cosine mode contributes the mean times the square root of the interval length.
$$c_0=L^{-1/2}\int_0^L f(x)\,dx.$$
Each family separately meets the orthonormality and completeness hypotheses of Parseval, so applying the identity once in each basis gives the two norm sums.

provides the two complete normalized bases, including the constant cosine mode

title: Fixed-endpoint variation
summary: For $q_\epsilon=q+\epsilon\eta$ with $\eta(t_1)=\eta(t_2)=0$, the first variation is $\delta S=(d/d\epsilon)S[q_\epsilon]|_{\epsilon=0}$.
body:
For $q_\epsilon=q+\epsilon\eta$ with $\eta(t_1)=\eta(t_2)=0$, the first variation is $\delta S=(d/d\epsilon)S[q_\epsilon]|_{\epsilon=0}$.

A stationary trajectory makes the first variation vanish for every admissible variation.

title: Fundamental lemma of variations
summary: If continuous $f$ satisfies $\int_a^b f\eta\,dt=0$ for every $\eta\in C_c^\infty(a,b)$, then $f=0$ on $(a,b)$.
body:
If continuous $f$ satisfies $\int_a^b f\eta\,dt=0$ for every $\eta\in C_c^\infty(a,b)$, then $f=0$ on $(a,b)$.

The same test applies separately to each real component.
proof:
Suppose the function is positive at an interior point. Continuity gives an open interval on which it is bounded below by a positive constant.
$$f(t)\ge m>0\qquad(t\in I).$$
Choose a nonnegative bump supported in that interval with positive integral.
$$\int_a^bf(t)\eta(t)\,dt\ge m\int_I\eta(t)\,dt>0.$$
This contradicts the hypothesis. Applying the argument to the negative of the function excludes negative values.

title: Retarded spherical kernel
summary: In free space $(\nabla^2-c^{-2}\partial_t^2)[f(t-R/c)/R]=-4\pi f(t)\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf R)$ for smooth $f$.
body:
In free space $(\nabla^2-c^{-2}\partial_t^2)[f(t-R/c)/R]=-4\pi f(t)\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf R)$ for smooth $f$.

Retarded time selects propagation outwards from the spatial origin.
proof:
Away from the origin the radial Laplacian follows by dividing the radial flux derivative by the spherical area.
$$u=\frac{f(t-R/c)}{R},\qquad \nabla^2u=\frac1R\partial_R^2(Ru)=\frac{f''(t-R/c)}{c^2R}=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u.$$
To evaluate the singular part, pair with a smooth spatial test function and integrate by parts outside a ball of radius $a$. The inner boundary normal for the exterior points inward.
$$\int_{R>a}(u\nabla^2\phi-\phi\nabla^2u)\,d^3R=\int_{R=a}(\phi\,\partial_Ru-u\,\partial_R\phi)\,da.$$
The second surface term is of order $a$; the first samples the central value.
$$a^2\partial_Ru=-f(t-a/c)-(a/c)f'(t-a/c)\longrightarrow-f(t).$$
The omitted time derivative is locally integrable and contributes order $a^2$ inside the ball. Taking the limit gives the delta source.
$$\langle(\nabla^2-c^{-2}\partial_t^2)u,\phi\rangle=-4\pi f(t)\phi(\mathbf 0).$$

identifies the point distribution

title: Lorentz force
summary: The fields $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ determine the force on a test charge through $\mathbf F=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)$.
body:
The fields $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ determine the force on a test charge through $\mathbf F=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)$.

In a specified inertial frame, measure force at fixed position and time in the limit of negligible disturbance by the test charge.
The force per unit charge at rest determines the electric field.
Measurements with several independent test velocities determine the magnetic field from the velocity-dependent force.

title: Electric and magnetic fields
summary: In an inertial frame, test charges measure $\mathbf E=\mathbf F(\mathbf 0)/q$ and $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B=[\mathbf F(\mathbf v)-\mathbf F(\mathbf 0)]/q$.
body:
In an inertial frame, test charges measure $\mathbf E=\mathbf F(\mathbf 0)/q$ and $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B=[\mathbf F(\mathbf v)-\mathbf F(\mathbf 0)]/q$.

Measure the electromagnetic force on a weak test charge at a fixed event for several velocities. Compare the results in the limit of negligible disturbance.
$$\mathbf E=\lim_{q\to0}\mathbf F(\mathbf0)/q,\qquad \mathbf v\times\mathbf B=\lim_{q\to0}[\mathbf F(\mathbf v)-\mathbf F(\mathbf0)]/q.$$
Two nonparallel velocity directions determine all components of the magnetic field.

title: Charge and current density
summary: The charge in a volume is $\int_\Omega\rho\,d^3r$, and the current through an oriented surface is $\int_\Sigma\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a$.
body:
The charge in a volume is $\int_\Omega\rho\,d^3r$, and the current through an oriented surface is $\int_\Sigma\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a$.

For species of number density $n_s$, charge $q_s$ and mean velocity $\mathbf v_s$, the densities add.
$$\rho=\sum_s q_s n_s,\qquad \mathbf J=\sum_s q_s n_s\mathbf v_s.$$
The continuum formulas include point sources through the Dirac delta.

title: Electric and magnetic flux and circulation
summary: For stationary surfaces, $\Phi_E=Q_{\rm enc}/\epsilon_0$ and $\Phi_B=0$ on closed surfaces, while $\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-\dot\Phi_B$ and $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0(I+\epsilon_0\dot\Phi_E)$ on boundary loops.
body:
For stationary surfaces, $\Phi_E=Q_{\rm enc}/\epsilon_0$ and $\Phi_B=0$ on closed surfaces, while $\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-\dot\Phi_B$ and $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0(I+\epsilon_0\dot\Phi_E)$ on boundary loops.

For an oriented surface $S$ with boundary $C$, write $\Phi_F(S)=\int_S\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf a$ and $I(S)=\int_S\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a$. For a closed surface use the outward normal and take $Q_{\rm enc}$ inside it. For a loop use the positively oriented boundary and the flux through its spanning surface.
assumptions: Piecewise smooth stationary regions and fields regular enough for the stated integrations.
proof:
Integrate the two divergence equations over a volume and apply the divergence theorem with outward normals.
$$\oint_{\partial\Omega}\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf a=\frac{1}{\epsilon_0}\int_\Omega\rho\,d^3r,\qquad \oint_{\partial\Omega}\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf a=0.$$
Integrate each curl equation over a surface and apply Stokes’ theorem with its induced boundary orientation.
$$\oint_{\partial\Sigma}\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_\Sigma\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf a.$$
$$\oint_{\partial\Sigma}\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0\int_\Sigma\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a+\mu_0\epsilon_0\frac{d}{dt}\int_\Sigma\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf a.$$
The surfaces are fixed in the chosen frame, so the time derivative passes through their integrals.

relations.basis: supplies the four local laws
converts volume and surface derivatives into boundary integrals
permits differentiation through a stationary integral

title: Local charge conservation
summary: Maxwell’s equations require $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$.
body: Maxwell’s equations require $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$.
assumptions: Derivatives commute, classically for smooth fields or in the distributional sense.
proof:
Take the divergence of the Ampère–Maxwell equation.
$$\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf B)=\mu_0\nabla\cdot\mathbf J+\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t(\nabla\cdot\mathbf E).$$
The contracted second derivatives vanish because interchanging the derivative indices reverses the alternating tensor.
$$\epsilon_{ijk}\partial_i\partial_j B_k=0.$$
Insert Gauss’s law and divide by the permeability to obtain local conservation.
$$\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0.$$
The divergence theorem therefore equates loss of enclosed charge to outward current.
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_\Omega\rho\,d^3r=-\oint_{\partial\Omega}\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a.$$

title: Scalar and vector potentials
summary: Potentials represent the fields by $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf E=-\nabla V-\partial_t\mathbf A$.
body:
Potentials represent the fields by $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf E=-\nabla V-\partial_t\mathbf A$.

A gauge transformation generated by a smooth scalar $\chi$ leaves the represented fields invariant.
$$\mathbf A'=\mathbf A+\nabla\chi,\qquad V'=V-\partial_t\chi.$$
The curl of a gradient vanishes by equality of mixed derivatives and the two new time derivatives cancel in the electric field.
For electrostatic fields choose a time-independent vector potential and use the voltage difference along any path in the patch.
$$V(b)-V(a)=-\int_a^b\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell.$$

title: Local existence of electromagnetic potentials
summary: On a smooth star-shaped spatial patch, the homogeneous Maxwell equations admit $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf E=-\nabla V-\partial_t\mathbf A$.
body: On a smooth star-shaped spatial patch, the homogeneous Maxwell equations admit $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf E=-\nabla V-\partial_t\mathbf A$.
assumptions: Smooth fields on a star-shaped patch at each time.
proof:
Choose the origin at a star centre and integrate the magnetic field along each radial segment at fixed time.
$$\mathbf A(\mathbf r,t)=-\int_0^1 s\,\mathbf r\times\mathbf B(s\mathbf r,t)\,ds.$$
Expanding the curl in components and using the zero magnetic divergence makes the integrand a radial derivative.
$$\nabla\times[-s\,\mathbf r\times\mathbf B(s\mathbf r,t)]=2s\mathbf B(s\mathbf r,t)+s^2(\mathbf r\cdot\nabla_{\!s\mathbf r})\mathbf B(s\mathbf r,t)=\frac{d}{ds}[s^2\mathbf B(s\mathbf r,t)].$$
Integration gives the prescribed magnetic field.
$$\nabla\times\mathbf A=\mathbf B.$$
Faraday’s law makes the corrected electric field curl-free.
$$\mathbf C=\mathbf E+\partial_t\mathbf A,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf C=0.$$
Set the potential to the negative radial line integral.
$$V(\mathbf r,t)=-\int_0^1 r_j C_j(s\mathbf r,t)\,ds.$$
Symmetry of its mixed field derivatives gives the required gradient component by component.
$$-\partial_i V=\int_0^1[C_i+s r_j\partial_j C_i]\,ds=\int_0^1\frac{d}{ds}[s C_i(s\mathbf r,t)]\,ds=C_i(\mathbf r,t).$$

relations.basis: specifies the required representation
supplies the two homogeneous field equations
integrates the radial derivatives

title: Electric and magnetic dipole moments
summary: For localized charge and steady current distributions, $\mathbf p=\int\mathbf r'\rho\,d^3r'$ and $\mathbf m=\tfrac12\int\mathbf r'\times\mathbf J\,d^3r'$.
body:
For localized charge and steady current distributions, $\mathbf p=\int\mathbf r'\rho\,d^3r'$ and $\mathbf m=\tfrac12\int\mathbf r'\times\mathbf J\,d^3r'$.

For a pair of opposite charges let $\mathbf d$ point from the negative charge to the positive charge.
$$\mathbf p=q\mathbf d.$$
Shifting the coordinate origin by $\mathbf a$ changes the electric moment by the net charge times that shift.
$$\mathbf p'=\int(\mathbf r'-\mathbf a)\rho\,d^3r'=\mathbf p-Q\mathbf a,\qquad Q=\int\rho\,d^3r'.$$
For a thin planar loop carrying steady current $I$, the magnetic moment equals current times oriented area.
$$\mathbf m=\frac I2\oint\mathbf r'\times d\boldsymbol\ell'=I\mathbf a_{\rm loop}.$$
Each directed boundary segment contributes its signed triangular area with respect to the chosen origin.

relations.basis: supplies the charge and current distributions

title: Polarization, magnetization and auxiliary fields
summary: The dipole moment densities $\mathbf P$ and $\mathbf M$ define $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P$ and $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0-\mathbf M$.
body:
The dipole moment densities $\mathbf P$ and $\mathbf M$ define $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P$ and $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0-\mathbf M$.

Polarization is electric dipole moment per unit volume and magnetization is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume after averaging over many microscopic constituents.
Treat the dipole densities as zero outside a finite body when derivatives include surface distributions.

relations.basis: identifies the microscopic moments being averaged
identifies the electric and magnetic fields

title: Sources of a continuous distribution of dipoles
summary: Electric and magnetic dipole densities give $\rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P$ and $\mathbf J_b=\partial_t\mathbf P+\nabla\times\mathbf M$ in the dipole model.
body: Electric and magnetic dipole densities give $\rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P$ and $\mathbf J_b=\partial_t\mathbf P+\nabla\times\mathbf M$ in the dipole model.
assumptions: Matter is at rest and represented by point electric dipoles at fixed centres and localized current loops in the magnetic dipole approximation.
proof:
Pair a small electric dipole with a smooth test function and expand about its centre.
$$q[f(\mathbf r_+)-f(\mathbf r_-)]=\mathbf p\cdot\nabla f(\mathbf r_c)+O(q|\mathbf d|^2).$$
Summing the leading moments and integrating by parts identifies the charge distribution.
$$\int\rho_b f\,d^3r=\int\mathbf P\cdot\nabla f\,d^3r=-\int f\nabla\cdot\mathbf P\,d^3r.$$
For fixed dipole centres the signed charge velocities add to the rate of change of electric dipole moment, which gives the polarization current to leading order in the electric dipole expansion.
$$q(\dot{\mathbf r}_+-\dot{\mathbf r}_-)=\dot{\mathbf p},\qquad \mathbf J_P=\partial_t\mathbf P.$$
Pair each elementary steady current loop with a smooth vector test field and apply Stokes’ theorem.
$$I\oint\mathbf f\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=I\int_{\Sigma}(\nabla\times\mathbf f)\cdot d\mathbf a\simeq\mathbf m\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf f)(\mathbf r_c).$$
Sum the point-dipole contributions and integrate by parts componentwise.
$$\int\mathbf J_M\cdot\mathbf f\,d^3r=\int\mathbf M\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf f)\,d^3r=\int(\nabla\times\mathbf M)\cdot\mathbf f\,d^3r.$$
Adding the two currents gives the bound current in this model.
$$\mathbf J_b=\partial_t\mathbf P+\nabla\times\mathbf M.$$

converts loop circulation to a curl and permits integration by parts
interprets the point-dipole sources through test functions

title: Macroscopic Maxwell equations
summary: The auxiliary fields satisfy $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f+\partial_t\mathbf D$.
body: The auxiliary fields satisfy $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f+\partial_t\mathbf D$.
assumptions: A macroscopic average commutes with differentiation in the dipole model.
proof:
Separate the total averaged charge and current into free and bound contributions.
$$\rho=\rho_f-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P,\qquad \mathbf J=\mathbf J_f+\partial_t\mathbf P+\nabla\times\mathbf M.$$
Gauss’s law groups the polarization with the vacuum electric term.
$$\nabla\cdot(\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P)=\rho_f.$$
The Ampère–Maxwell equation groups the magnetization with the magnetic field and the polarization with the displacement current.
$$\nabla\times(\mathbf B/\mu_0-\mathbf M)=\mathbf J_f+\partial_t(\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P).$$
Substituting the definitions of the auxiliary fields yields both equations.

relations.basis: identifies charge and current carried by bound dipoles
supplies Gauss and Ampère–Maxwell equations
names the two auxiliary fields

title: Permittivity and permeability
summary: For linear, isotropic, local, instantaneous response without permanent polarization or magnetization, $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$.
body:
For linear, isotropic, local, instantaneous response without permanent polarization or magnetization, $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$.

The response coefficients follow by substituting the susceptibilities into the auxiliary-field definitions.
$$\mathbf P=\epsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E,\qquad\mathbf M=\chi_m\mathbf H,\qquad \epsilon=\epsilon_0(1+\chi_e),\qquad \mu=\mu_0(1+\chi_m).$$
Anisotropy can require tensors and dispersion makes the coefficients frequency-dependent.

relations.basis: provides the fields in the constitutive relations

title: SI metre
summary: The SI defines the metre by fixing the vacuum speed of light to $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ exactly.
body:
The SI defines the metre by fixing the vacuum speed of light to $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ exactly.

With the SI second established by the caesium frequency, one metre equals the path traversed in vacuum by light during $1/299\,792\,458$ of a second.

title: Vacuum electromagnetic wave speed
summary: Electromagnetic waves in empty space travel at $c=(\mu_0\epsilon_0)^{-1/2}$, whose exact SI value is $299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
body: Electromagnetic waves in empty space travel at $c=(\mu_0\epsilon_0)^{-1/2}$, whose exact SI value is $299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
assumptions: Source-free vacuum with constant positive $\epsilon_0,\mu_0$ and nonzero wave curvature.
proof:
Curl Faraday’s law and use the source-free Ampère–Maxwell law to eliminate the magnetic field.
$$\nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf E)=-\partial_t(\nabla\times\mathbf B)=-\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t^2\mathbf E.$$
Contracting two alternating tensors and commuting partial derivatives gives the double-curl identity.
$$[\nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf E)]_i=(\delta_{il}\delta_{jm}-\delta_{im}\delta_{jl})\partial_j\partial_l E_m=\partial_i\partial_j E_j-\nabla^2 E_i.$$
The electric divergence vanishes by the vacuum Gauss law.
$$\nabla^2\mathbf E=\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t^2\mathbf E.$$
A transverse profile propagating along a unit direction solves this equation if its spatial and temporal curvature terms agree.
$$\mathbf E=\mathbf e f(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r-vt),\qquad |\mathbf n|=1,\quad\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e=0.$$
$$(1-\mu_0\epsilon_0 v^2)\mathbf e f''=0,\qquad c=|v|=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}.$$
The companion magnetic field follows from the two curl equations for propagation in the positive direction.
$$\mathbf B=\frac1c\,\mathbf n\times\mathbf E.$$
The SI fixes the numerical value of the speed through the definition of the metre.

expands the two curls
differentiates a translating profile
sets the numerical value in SI after the wave speed has been derived

title: Retarded potentials
summary: An isolated source in vacuum gives $V=(4\pi\epsilon_0)^{-1}\int [\rho]/R\,d^3r'$ and $\mathbf A=(\mu_0/4\pi)\int [\mathbf J]/R\,d^3r'$ in the retarded Lorenz gauge.
body: An isolated source in vacuum gives $V=(4\pi\epsilon_0)^{-1}\int [\rho]/R\,d^3r'$ and $\mathbf A=(\mu_0/4\pi)\int [\mathbf J]/R\,d^3r'$ in the retarded Lorenz gauge.
assumptions: Localized conserved sources in unbounded vacuum with convergent integrals and retarded data excluding free fields.
proof:
Write brackets for evaluation at the time when a signal must leave the source point to reach the observation event.
$$R=|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|,\qquad [f]=f(\mathbf r',t-R/c),\qquad \Box=\nabla^2-c^{-2}\partial_t^2.$$
Choose the Lorenz gauge, insert the potentials into Gauss’s law and collect scalar derivatives.
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf A=-c^{-2}\partial_t V,\qquad -\nabla^2V-\partial_t\nabla\cdot\mathbf A=\rho/\epsilon_0,\qquad \Box V=-\rho/\epsilon_0.$$
The Ampère–Maxwell law and double-curl identity group its mixed terms into the same gauge combination.
$$\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf A+c^{-2}\partial_t V)-\Box\mathbf A=\mu_0\mathbf J,\qquad \Box\mathbf A=-\mu_0\mathbf J.$$
The retarded spherical kernel generates a point source for each fixed integration point.
$$\Box\frac{[f]}{R}=-4\pi f(\mathbf r',t)\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf r').$$
Superpose these sources with the required coefficients to get the scalar and vector potentials.
$$V(\mathbf r,t)=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int\frac{[\rho]}{R}\,d^3r',\qquad \mathbf A(\mathbf r,t)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{[\mathbf J]}{R}\,d^3r'.$$
To verify the gauge, transfer the spatial derivative of the translation-invariant retarded convolution kernel to the source by integration by parts.
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf A+c^{-2}\partial_t V=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{[\nabla'\cdot\mathbf J+\partial_t\rho]}{R}\,d^3r'=0.$$
Charge conservation makes this last integrand vanish and the retarded initial or boundary data exclude an added homogeneous wave.

title: Current and the changing electric dipole
summary: For localized conserved charge, $\dot{\mathbf p}=\int\mathbf J\,d^3r'$.
body: For localized conserved charge, $\dot{\mathbf p}=\int\mathbf J\,d^3r'$.
assumptions: Localization makes the boundary term vanish and permits differentiation of the dipole integral.
proof:
Differentiate one Cartesian component of the electric dipole and insert charge continuity.
$$\dot p_i=\int r'_i\partial_t\rho\,d^3r'=-\int r'_i\partial'_j J_j\,d^3r'.$$
Integrate by parts and drop the boundary integral where the current vanishes.
$$\dot p_i=-\lim_{a\to\infty}\oint_{|\mathbf r'|=a}r'_i\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a'+\int(\partial'_j r'_i)J_j\,d^3r'=\int J_i\,d^3r'.$$

title: Far-zone electric dipole radiation
summary: At retarded time $t_r=t-r/c$ the leading electric dipole terms are $\mathbf E_{\rm rad}=\mathbf n\times(\mathbf n\times\ddot{\mathbf p})/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^2r)$ and $\mathbf B_{\rm rad}=\mathbf n\times\mathbf E_{\rm rad}/c$.
body: At retarded time $t_r=t-r/c$ the leading electric dipole terms are $\mathbf E_{\rm rad}=\mathbf n\times(\mathbf n\times\ddot{\mathbf p})/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^2r)$ and $\mathbf B_{\rm rad}=\mathbf n\times\mathbf E_{\rm rad}/c$.
assumptions: Localized neutral source in vacuum with $a\ll c\tau\ll r$, smooth time dependence and retarded fields.
proof:
Let the source have size $a$ and characteristic time $\tau$ and place the origin inside it.
$$r=|\mathbf r|,\qquad\mathbf n=\mathbf r/r,\qquad a\ll c\tau\ll r,\qquad t_r=t-r/c.$$
The far-zone expansion separates the common propagation delay from the direction-dependent delay across the source.
$$R=r-\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r'+O(a^2/r),\qquad R^{-1}=r^{-1}+O(a/r^2).$$
Keep first order in the delay for the charge density and zeroth order for the current density in the leading electric dipole approximation.
$$[\rho]\simeq\rho(\mathbf r',t_r)+(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r'/c)\partial_t\rho(\mathbf r',t_r),\qquad [\mathbf J]\simeq\mathbf J(\mathbf r',t_r).$$
The net charge vanishes and the current integral equals the first time derivative of the dipole.
$$V_{\rm dip}^{(1/r)}=\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\dot{\mathbf p}(t_r)}{4\pi\epsilon_0cr},\qquad \mathbf A_{\rm dip}^{(1/r)}=\frac{\mu_0\dot{\mathbf p}(t_r)}{4\pi r}.$$
Spatial differentiation of the retarded argument contributes at order $1/r$, while differentiating the direction or radial prefactor contributes at order $1/r^2$.
$$\nabla t_r=-\frac{\mathbf n}{c},\qquad \mathbf E_{\rm rad}=\left[-\nabla V-\partial_t\mathbf A\right]_{\rm rad}=\frac{\mathbf n(\mathbf n\cdot\ddot{\mathbf p})-\ddot{\mathbf p}}{4\pi\epsilon_0c^2r}.$$
Curling the vector potential gives the transverse magnetic field at the same order.
$$\mathbf B_{\rm rad}=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi cr}\mathbf n\times\ddot{\mathbf p}=\frac{\mathbf n\times\mathbf E_{\rm rad}}{c}.$$
The expression gives the electric dipole contribution, which can vanish even when higher multipoles radiate.

title: Poynting’s theorem
summary: Microscopic fields obey $\partial_t u+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$, with $u=\epsilon_0|\mathbf E|^2/2+|\mathbf B|^2/(2\mu_0)$ and $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/\mu_0$.
body: Microscopic fields obey $\partial_t u+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$, with $u=\epsilon_0|\mathbf E|^2/2+|\mathbf B|^2/(2\mu_0)$ and $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/\mu_0$.
assumptions: Microscopic total sources in SI and regular fields for the stated products and integrals.
proof:
Taking the scalar product of the Lorentz force with charge velocity eliminates the magnetic force, which is perpendicular to that velocity.
$$\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=q\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf v,\qquad \sum_s n_s q_s\mathbf v_s\cdot\mathbf E=\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E.$$
The product rule for the divergence of a cross product follows by grouping the derivative of each factor in components.
$$\partial_i(\epsilon_{ijk}E_j B_k)=\mathbf B\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)-\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf B).$$
Substitute both Maxwell curl equations and divide by the vacuum permeability.
$$\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}\right)=-\frac{\mathbf B\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B}{\mu_0}-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E-\epsilon_0\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf E.$$
Group the derivatives of the squared fields to identify energy stored per unit volume and power transported per unit area.
$$\partial_t\left(\frac{\epsilon_0|\mathbf E|^2}{2}+\frac{|\mathbf B|^2}{2\mu_0}\right)+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E.$$
The divergence theorem gives the balance for a fixed volume with an outward-oriented boundary.
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_\Omega u\,d^3r=-\oint_{\partial\Omega}\mathbf S\cdot d\mathbf a-\int_\Omega\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\,d^3r.$$

title: Electric dipole radiation power
summary: The instantaneous outward electric dipole power is $P(t)=|\ddot{\mathbf p}(t-r/c)|^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0 c^3)$ on a far-zone sphere.
body: The instantaneous outward electric dipole power is $P(t)=|\ddot{\mathbf p}(t-r/c)|^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0 c^3)$ on a far-zone sphere.
assumptions: Leading electric dipole radiation in vacuum on a sphere in the radiation zone.
proof:
For transverse radiation fields the vector triple product makes the Poynting vector radial.
$$\mathbf S_{\rm rad}=\frac{\mathbf E_{\rm rad}\times(\mathbf n\times\mathbf E_{\rm rad})}{\mu_0c}=\epsilon_0c|\mathbf E_{\rm rad}|^2\mathbf n.$$
Take the polar axis along the dipole acceleration at the retarded time, so the transverse projection has magnitude $|\ddot{\mathbf p}|\sin\theta$.
$$\frac{dP}{d\Omega}=r^2\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf S_{\rm rad}=\frac{|\ddot{\mathbf p}(t-r/c)|^2\sin^2\theta}{16\pi^2\epsilon_0c^3}.$$
Integrate over the sphere using the cosine of polar angle as variable.
$$\int\sin^2\theta\,d\Omega=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^2)\,du=\frac{8\pi}{3}.$$
This gives the instantaneous dipole power, with zero flux when the dipole acceleration vanishes.
$$P(t)=\int\frac{dP}{d\Omega}\,d\Omega=\frac{|\ddot{\mathbf p}(t-r/c)|^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0 c^3}.$$

title: State ray and wave function
summary: A pure-state ray has normalized representatives $e^{i\alpha}|\psi\rangle$ and position amplitude $\psi(x)=\langle x|\psi\rangle$.
body:
A pure-state ray has normalized representatives $e^{i\alpha}|\psi\rangle$ and position amplitude $\psi(x)=\langle x|\psi\rangle$.

For a spinless particle on a line the position representation identifies normalized state vectors with square-integrable amplitudes modulo equality almost everywhere.
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|\psi(x)|^2\,dx=1,\qquad \psi\sim e^{i\alpha}\psi,\quad \alpha\in\mathbb R.$$

title: Pure states and the Born rule
summary: A normalized ray represents a pure state, and the probability for a projector $P$ is $\langle\psi|P|\psi\rangle$.
body:
A normalized ray represents a pure state, and the probability for a projector $P$ is $\langle\psi|P|\psi\rangle$.

Unit vectors differing by a global phase represent the same preparation.
$$\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=1,\qquad |\psi\rangle\sim e^{i\alpha}|\psi\rangle,\qquad\alpha\in\mathbb R.$$
In the position representation the projector onto a region multiplies by its indicator, so the Born rule assigns the integrated squared amplitude to that region.
$$\psi(x)=\langle x|\psi\rangle,\qquad \Pr(x\in I)=\int_I|\psi(x)|^2\,dx.$$

title: Linear, symmetric and self-adjoint operators
summary: A quantum observable is a linear operator equal to its adjoint, $A=A^\dagger$ with $D(A)=D(A^\dagger)$.
body:
A quantum observable is a linear operator equal to its adjoint, $A=A^\dagger$ with $D(A)=D(A^\dagger)$.

Linearity holds for vectors in the domain and complex scalars.
$$A(a\psi+b\phi)=aA\psi+bA\phi.$$
For a densely defined operator the adjoint domain consists of vectors $\phi$ for which there is a vector $\eta$ giving the following pairing for every $\psi\in D(A)$.
$$\langle\phi|A\psi\rangle=\langle\eta|\psi\rangle,\qquad A^\dagger\phi=\eta.$$
Symmetry means the operator agrees with its adjoint on its own domain, while self-adjointness requires equality of domains as well.
$$A\subseteq A^\dagger\quad\text{(symmetric)},\qquad A=A^\dagger\quad\text{(self-adjoint)}.$$
A finite matrix on the whole space is self-adjoint exactly when it equals its conjugate transpose.

body:
An isolated nonrelativistic state evolves by $i\hbar\,d|\psi\rangle/dt=H(t)|\psi\rangle$.

The Hamiltonian is the energy observable and the generator of time evolution.
Use states in the operator domain for the differential equation and assume the Hamiltonian generates unitary evolution on the time interval considered.

title: Spatial translations and their generator
summary: A rightward translation by $a$ acts as $(T(a)\psi)(x)=\psi(x-a)$, and its generator is the canonical momentum $p$.
body:
A rightward translation by $a$ acts as $(T(a)\psi)(x)=\psi(x-a)$, and its generator is the canonical momentum $p$.

For states differentiable under translations, define the generator by its strong derivative.
$$p\psi=i\hbar\lim_{a\to0}\frac{T(a)\psi-\psi}{a}.$$
The translated probability density therefore takes its old value at the point displaced to the left by the same amount.

title: Position-space momentum
summary: For canonical translations on the real line the momentum acts as $p=-i\hbar\,\partial_x$.
body: For canonical translations on the real line the momentum acts as $p=-i\hbar\,\partial_x$.
assumptions: Full real line and the usual translation representation on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ with momentum domain $H^1(\mathbb R)$.
proof:
Translate a smooth compactly supported state and form its first-order difference quotient.
$$\frac{(T(a)\psi)(x)-\psi(x)}{a}=\frac{\psi(x-a)-\psi(x)}{a}=-\int_0^1\psi'(x-sa)\,ds.$$
The translated derivative converges in the square-integrable norm to the original derivative, so the defining generator acts as stated.
$$p\psi=-i\hbar\,\psi'.$$
The same integral argument extends to absolutely continuous representatives with square-integrable weak derivative, using continuity of translations in the square-integrable norm.

title: Scalar-potential particle Hamiltonian
summary: A spinless nonrelativistic particle of constant mass in a local potential has $H=p^2/(2m)+V(X,t)$ in one Cartesian coordinate.
body:
A spinless nonrelativistic particle of constant mass in a local potential has $H=p^2/(2m)+V(X,t)$ in one Cartesian coordinate.

In the position representation the position operator $X$ and functions of it multiply the wave function.
$$(X\psi)(x)=x\psi(x),\qquad (V(X,t)\psi)(x)=V(x,t)\psi(x).$$
In three Cartesian coordinates the kinetic term sums the squared canonical momenta and the potential multiplies at the observation point.

title: Position-space Schrödinger equation
summary: For a scalar local potential $i\hbar\partial_t\psi=-(\hbar^2/2m)\partial_x^2\psi+V\psi$.
body: For a scalar local potential $i\hbar\partial_t\psi=-(\hbar^2/2m)\partial_x^2\psi+V\psi$.
assumptions: Constant positive mass, a time-independent Cartesian basis, a scalar local potential and sufficient regularity for the derivatives.
proof:
Project the state equation onto the time-independent position basis.
$$i\hbar\partial_t\psi(x,t)=\langle x|H|\psi(t)\rangle.$$
Insert the scalar-potential Hamiltonian and apply the momentum operator twice.
$$(p^2\psi)(x)=(-i\hbar)^2\partial_x^2\psi(x)=-\hbar^2\partial_x^2\psi(x).$$
Combining kinetic and potential terms gives the coordinate equation.
$$i\hbar\partial_t\psi(x,t)=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2\psi(x,t)+V(x,t)\psi(x,t).$$
Summing the three Cartesian kinetic terms replaces the one-dimensional second derivative by $\nabla^2$.

title: Stationary energy eigenstates
summary: For a time-independent Hamiltonian a state of definite energy evolves as $|\psi(t)\rangle=e^{-iE(t-t_0)/\hbar}|u_E\rangle$.
body: For a time-independent Hamiltonian a state of definite energy evolves as $|\psi(t)\rangle=e^{-iE(t-t_0)/\hbar}|u_E\rangle$.
assumptions: Time-independent self-adjoint Hamiltonian and an energy eigenvector in its domain.
proof:
Insert a fixed eigenvector times a scalar time factor into the state equation.
$$H|u_E\rangle=E|u_E\rangle,\qquad |\psi(t)\rangle=f(t)|u_E\rangle,\qquad i\hbar\dot f=Ef.$$
Integrate the scalar equation with a unit initial factor.
$$f(t)=\exp[-iE(t-t_0)/\hbar].$$
Self-adjointness makes the eigenvalue real, so this phase leaves the probability of every fixed measurement outcome unchanged.
$$\langle u_E|Hu_E\rangle=E\langle u_E|u_E\rangle=E^*\langle u_E|u_E\rangle.$$

title: Free plane waves
summary: In a constant potential a generalized plane wave $\psi=Ae^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ has $\hbar\omega=\hbar^2 k^2/(2m)+V_0$.
body: In a constant potential a generalized plane wave $\psi=Ae^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ has $\hbar\omega=\hbar^2 k^2/(2m)+V_0$.
assumptions: Real constant potential on the line and real wave number.
proof:
Act with time and space derivatives on the travelling phase.
$$\partial_t\psi=-i\omega\psi,\qquad \partial_x^2\psi=-k^2\psi.$$
Substitute these derivatives into the wave equation and divide out the nonzero amplitude.
$$\hbar\omega=\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}+V_0.$$
The momentum derivative and the time phase identify the momentum and energy of the mode.
$$p\psi=\hbar k\psi,\qquad E=\hbar\omega.$$
These modes have constant density on the whole line and represent generalized eigenfunctions used to form wave packets.

title: Infinite square well
summary: For zero potential on $(0,L)$ with hard walls, $u_n=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$ and $E_n=\hbar^2\pi^2 n^2/(2mL^2)$ for $n=1,2,\ldots$.
body: For zero potential on $(0,L)$ with hard walls, $u_n=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$ and $E_n=\hbar^2\pi^2 n^2/(2mL^2)$ for $n=1,2,\ldots$.
assumptions: Positive mass, $L>0$ and the Dirichlet kinetic Hamiltonian on a finite interval.
proof:
The infinite walls impose Dirichlet endpoints, and separation of the time phase gives the interior eigenproblem.
$$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}u''=Eu,\qquad u(0)=u(L)=0.$$
Multiply by the conjugate, integrate by parts and use both endpoint values to determine the sign of the energy.
$$E\int_0^L |u|^2dx=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int_0^L |u'|^2dx>0.$$
Equality would require a constant function with both endpoint values zero, so every eigenstate has a positive wave number.
$$k=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar,\qquad u=A\sin(kx)+B\cos(kx).$$
The first wall eliminates the cosine and the second quantizes the sine.
$$B=0,\qquad \sin(kL)=0,\qquad k_n=n\pi/L,\qquad n=1,2,\ldots.$$
Normalize using the integral of the squared sine and restore the separated time factor.
$$\int_0^L\sin^2(k_nx)\,dx=L/2,\qquad \psi_n(x,t)=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(k_nx)e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}.$$
The Fourier sine basis spans square-integrable states inside the well, and the idealized spatial wave functions vanish outside.

title: Probability current
summary: For real local potentials $\partial_t|\psi|^2+\partial_x j=0$, with $j=(\hbar/m)\operatorname{Im}(\psi^*\partial_x\psi)$.
body: For real local potentials $\partial_t|\psi|^2+\partial_x j=0$, with $j=(\hbar/m)\operatorname{Im}(\psi^*\partial_x\psi)$.
assumptions: Real local potential, constant mass, no vector potential and sufficient wave-function regularity.
proof:
Multiply the wave equation by the conjugate amplitude and its complex conjugate by the original amplitude.
$$i\hbar\psi^*\partial_t\psi=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi^*\psi''+V|\psi|^2,\qquad -i\hbar\psi\partial_t\psi^*=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi\psi^{*\,\prime\prime}+V|\psi|^2.$$
Subtract the conjugated equation to cancel the real potential and use the product rule on each side.
$$i\hbar\partial_t|\psi|^2=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x(\psi^*\psi'-\psi\psi^{*\,\prime}).$$
Dividing by the imaginary coefficient yields the continuity equation for the Born density.
$$j=\frac{\hbar}{2mi}(\psi^*\psi'-\psi\psi^{*\,\prime}),\qquad \partial_t|\psi|^2=-\partial_x j.$$
An interval gains probability through its left endpoint and loses it through its right endpoint.
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b|\psi|^2dx=j(a,t)-j(b,t).$$

title: Matching at a finite potential step
summary: At an ordinary finite jump of the potential, both $u$ and $u'$ are continuous for a constant-mass stationary particle.
body: At an ordinary finite jump of the potential, both $u$ and $u'$ are continuous for a constant-mass stationary particle.
assumptions: Constant mass, finite piecewise continuous scalar potential and a locally bounded piecewise smooth wave function.
proof:
Near a step at the origin the spatial equation has a locally integrable right-hand side.
$$u''=\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}(V-E)u.$$
For a piecewise smooth wave function a jump would add singular terms to its distributional second derivative.
$$u''_{\rm dist}=u''_{\rm pieces}+[u']_0\,\delta(x)+[u]_0\,\delta'(x),\qquad [g]_0=g(0^+)-g(0^-).$$
The jump terms follow by integrating against a test function by parts twice on the two half intervals.
The finite potential times a locally bounded wave function carries neither singular term, so both jump coefficients vanish.
$$[u]_0=[u']_0=0.$$

title: Step reflection and transmission
summary: For a real step with both channels open, $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(k_2/k_1)|t|^2$ with $R+T=1$.
body: For a real step with both channels open, $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(k_2/k_1)|t|^2$ with $R+T=1$.
assumptions: Real finite step, equal positive mass on both sides, a single incident channel and $E>\max(V_1,V_2)$ for the propagating formulas.
proof:
Take a stationary wave incident from the left with unit amplitude and choose an outgoing transmitted wave on the right.
$$u_1=e^{ik_1x}+r e^{-ik_1x},\qquad u_2=t e^{ik_2x},\qquad k_j=\sqrt{2m(E-V_j)}/\hbar.$$
Match the wave and its derivative at the step and solve the two linear equations.
$$1+r=t,\qquad k_1(1-r)=k_2t.$$
$$r=\frac{k_1-k_2}{k_1+k_2},\qquad t=\frac{2k_1}{k_1+k_2}.$$
In the current of the incident and reflected superposition the two interference terms in $u^*u'$ combine to a real number.
$$j_{\rm in}=\hbar k_1/m,\qquad j_{\rm ref}=-(\hbar k_1/m)|r|^2,\qquad j_{\rm tr}=(\hbar k_2/m)|t|^2.$$
The outward flux magnitudes relative to incident flux give the fractions and their sum.
$$R=-j_{\rm ref}/j_{\rm in}=|r|^2,\qquad T=j_{\rm tr}/j_{\rm in}=(k_2/k_1)|t|^2.$$
$$R+T=\frac{(k_1-k_2)^2+4k_1k_2}{(k_1+k_2)^2}=1.$$
If the right half-line is evanescent, its bounded solution is a decaying real exponential times a complex constant and therefore carries zero current.

title: Canonical position–momentum commutator
summary: Cartesian position and canonical momentum satisfy $[X_i,p_j]=i\hbar\delta_{ij}$ on a common invariant test domain.
body: Cartesian position and canonical momentum satisfy $[X_i,p_j]=i\hbar\delta_{ij}$ on a common invariant test domain.
assumptions: A common test domain such as smooth rapidly decaying functions in Cartesian space.
proof:
Apply both operator products to a smooth test wave function.
$$(X_i p_j)\psi=-i\hbar x_i\partial_j\psi,\qquad (p_jX_i)\psi=-i\hbar(\delta_{ij}\psi+x_i\partial_j\psi).$$
Subtract these expressions and use commuting coordinate multipliers and commuting partial derivatives for the other pairs.
$$[X_i,p_j]\psi=i\hbar\delta_{ij}\psi,\qquad [X_i,X_j]\psi=[p_i,p_j]\psi=0.$$

title: Oscillator ladder operators
summary: The oscillator factors as $H=\hbar\omega(a^\dagger a+\tfrac12)$ and its ladder operators obey $[a,a^\dagger]=1$.
body: The oscillator factors as $H=\hbar\omega(a^\dagger a+\tfrac12)$ and its ladder operators obey $[a,a^\dagger]=1$.
assumptions: Positive mass and frequency and a common invariant domain for the oscillator products.
proof:
Define dimensionless lowering and raising operators for the oscillator with positive mass and frequency.
$$a=\frac{m\omega X+ip}{\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}},\qquad a^\dagger=\frac{m\omega X-ip}{\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}},\qquad H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2X^2}{2}.$$
Multiplying in each order reduces the mixed terms to the canonical commutator.
$$a^\dagger a=\frac{m^2\omega^2X^2+p^2+i m\omega[X,p]}{2m\hbar\omega}=\frac H{\hbar\omega}-\tfrac12,\qquad aa^\dagger=\frac H{\hbar\omega}+\tfrac12.$$
Subtract the products and commute each ladder operator through the factorized Hamiltonian.
$$[a,a^\dagger]=1,\qquad [H,a]=-\hbar\omega a,\qquad [H,a^\dagger]=\hbar\omega a^\dagger.$$
Adjointness and factorization give the norms after lowering and raising a normalized energy eigenvector.
$$\|a u\|^2=\frac E{\hbar\omega}-\tfrac12,\qquad\|a^\dagger u\|^2=\frac E{\hbar\omega}+\tfrac12.$$

title: Completeness of Gaussian-weighted polynomials
summary: For $\alpha>0$, the span of $x^n e^{-\alpha x^2/2}$ for $n\ge0$ is dense in $L^2(\mathbb R)$.
body: For $\alpha>0$, the span of $x^n e^{-\alpha x^2/2}$ for $n\ge0$ is dense in $L^2(\mathbb R)$.
assumptions: Positive Gaussian width parameter and Lebesgue square-integrability on the whole real line.
proof:
Take a square-integrable function orthogonal to each Gaussian-weighted power and multiply its complex conjugate by the Gaussian.
$$g(x)=f(x)^* e^{-\alpha x^2/2},\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}x^n g(x)\,dx=0\quad(n=0,1,\ldots).$$
Cauchy–Schwarz bounds every exponential moment in absolute value by a finite Gaussian integral.
$$\int |g(x)| e^{M|x|}\,dx\le\|f\|_2\left(\int e^{-\alpha x^2+2M|x|}\,dx\right)^{1/2}<\infty\qquad(M>0).$$
This bound permits integration of the series for an oscillatory exponential term by term, so the Fourier integral of the weighted function vanishes for every real wave number.
$$\hat g(k)=\int g(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(-ik)^n}{n!}\int x^n g(x)\,dx=0.$$
To see uniqueness directly, smooth the weighted function with a normalized Gaussian of width tending to zero.
$$K_s(y)=\frac{e^{-y^2/(4s)}}{\sqrt{4\pi s}}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-s k^2}e^{iky}\,dk,\qquad s>0.$$
The Gaussian integral on the right satisfies the same first-order equation and value at the origin as the expression on the left, by differentiating in $y$ and integrating by parts in $k$.
$$K_s'(y)=-\frac{y}{2s}K_s(y),\qquad K_s(0)=(4\pi s)^{-1/2}.$$
Absolute integrability permits exchanging the integrations, giving zero after Gaussian smoothing.
$$(g*K_s)(y)=\frac1{2\pi}\int e^{-sk^2}e^{iky}\hat g(k)\,dk=0.$$
For a smooth compactly supported test function $\phi$, uniform continuity makes $K_s*\phi$ converge uniformly to $\phi$ as the Gaussian mass outside every fixed neighborhood tends to zero.
$$\int g(x)\phi(x)\,dx=\lim_{s\downarrow0}\int (g*K_s)(y)\phi(y)\,dy=0.$$
Approximating a finite interval indicator by bounded smooth cutoffs and using dominated convergence shows that the integral of $g$ on every such interval is zero.
The absolutely continuous primitive of $g$ is constant, so $g$ vanishes almost everywhere, and the Gaussian factor is everywhere positive.
Thus the orthogonal complement of the stated span is zero, proving density in the Hilbert space.

title: Harmonic oscillator spectrum
summary: For the harmonic oscillator on the real line, $E_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)$ for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$.
body: For the harmonic oscillator on the real line, $E_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)$ for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$.
assumptions: The usual self-adjoint oscillator on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ with $m,\omega>0$; the ladder construction is on rapidly decaying smooth eigenfunctions.
proof:
The squared lowering norm bounds each energy eigenvalue below, while the commutator lowers the energy by one quantum whenever the result is nonzero.
$$E\ge\tfrac12\hbar\omega,\qquad H(au)=(E-\hbar\omega)au.$$
Repeated lowering must therefore terminate and its final nonzero state has zero lowering norm and the ground energy.
$$au_0=0,\qquad E_0=\tfrac12\hbar\omega.$$
In coordinate space the ground-state equation integrates to a Gaussian whose squared integral fixes its normalization.
$$\alpha=m\omega/\hbar,\qquad u_0'=-\alpha x u_0,\qquad u_0(x)=(\alpha/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-\alpha x^2/2}.$$
Repeated raising gives nonzero normalized eigenfunctions since the squared raising norm of level $n$ equals $n+1$.
$$u_n=\frac{(a^\dagger)^n}{\sqrt{n!}}u_0,\qquad Hu_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)u_n.$$
Acting on a polynomial times the ground Gaussian raises the polynomial degree by exactly one and keeps its leading coefficient nonzero.
$$a^\dagger(Pu_0)=\frac{2\alpha xP-P'}{\sqrt{2\alpha}}u_0.$$
The resulting polynomials span all polynomial degrees successively, and Gaussian-weighted polynomials are dense on the real line.
The complete energy eigenbasis and divergence of its eigenvalues to infinity exhaust the spectrum of the self-adjoint oscillator.

title: Orbital angular momentum and spin
summary: Orbital angular momentum is $\mathbf L=\mathbf X\times\mathbf p$, spin $\mathbf S$ acts on internal states and total angular momentum is $\mathbf J=\mathbf L+\mathbf S$.
body:
Orbital angular momentum is $\mathbf L=\mathbf X\times\mathbf p$, spin $\mathbf S$ acts on internal states and total angular momentum is $\mathbf J=\mathbf L+\mathbf S$.

The components of angular momentum are defined as generators of rotations with the right-handed infinitesimal rotation convention.
$$U_i(\theta)=\exp(-i\theta J_i/\hbar),\qquad [J_i,J_j]=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}J_k.$$
Spin is an internal representation of this rotation algebra and commutes with the orbital operators on the product space.
$$[L_i,S_j]=0,\qquad \mathbf J^2=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2.$$

defines the observable components

title: Electron spin g factor
summary: For a free electron, $\boldsymbol\mu=-g\mu_B\mathbf S/\hbar$ defines the spin factor $g$, with $\mu_B=e\hbar/(2m_e)$ and $e>0$.
body:
For a free electron, $\boldsymbol\mu=-g\mu_B\mathbf S/\hbar$ defines the spin factor $g$, with $\mu_B=e\hbar/(2m_e)$ and $e>0$.

For the state polarized along the measurement axis, the signed moment relative to the Bohr magneton determines the reported factor.
$$S_z=\hbar/2,\qquad -\mu_z/\mu_B=g/2.$$

title: Orbital rotation algebra
summary: Cartesian orbital generators obey $[L_i,L_j]=i\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$ and $L_z=-i\hbar\partial_\varphi$.
body: Cartesian orbital generators obey $[L_i,L_j]=i\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$ and $L_z=-i\hbar\partial_\varphi$.
assumptions: Smooth orbital wave functions in three-dimensional Cartesian space.
proof:
Use the canonical commutator to move each momentum past the other product’s coordinate.
$$[X_a p_b,X_c p_d]=-i\hbar\delta_{bc}X_a p_d+i\hbar\delta_{ad}X_c p_b.$$
For the first two Cartesian angular momenta only two product commutators survive, and cycling axes gives the remaining components.
$$[Yp_z-Zp_y,Zp_x-Xp_z]=i\hbar(Xp_y-Yp_x)=i\hbar L_z.$$
In cylindrical or spherical coordinates the derivative of a scalar wave function with respect to azimuth follows by the chain rule at fixed radius and polar angle.
$$\partial_\varphi=-y\partial_x+x\partial_y,\qquad L_z=Xp_y-Yp_x=-i\hbar\partial_\varphi.$$

title: Angular momentum quantum numbers
summary: In an irreducible rotation multiplet $\mathbf J^2=\hbar^2 j(j+1)$ and $J_z=\hbar m$ on joint eigenstates, with $m=-j,-j+1,\ldots,j$ and $2j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$.
body: In an irreducible rotation multiplet $\mathbf J^2=\hbar^2 j(j+1)$ and $J_z=\hbar m$ on joint eigenstates, with $m=-j,-j+1,\ldots,j$ and $2j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$.
assumptions: An irreducible unitary angular momentum multiplet generated from a joint weight vector, with adjoint ladder components on the common domain.
proof:
The rotation commutators give ladder operators that preserve the squared angular momentum and shift the axial component by one quantum.
$$J_\pm=J_x\pm iJ_y,\qquad[J_z,J_\pm]=\pm\hbar J_\pm,\qquad [\mathbf J^2,J_i]=i\hbar\sum_{k,l}\epsilon_{kil}(J_kJ_l+J_lJ_k)=0.$$
Take a normalized joint eigenstate with squared angular momentum eigenvalue $\hbar^2\lambda$ and axial eigenvalue $\hbar m$.
$$J_\mp J_\pm=\mathbf J^2-J_z^2\mp\hbar J_z,\qquad \|J_\pm u\|^2=\hbar^2[\lambda-m(m\pm1)].$$
Positivity bounds the allowed axial eigenvalues in either direction, so each unit-step ladder has a highest and lowest weight.
$$\lambda=m_{\rm high}(m_{\rm high}+1)=m_{\rm low}(m_{\rm low}-1).$$
Factoring the difference and using the ordering of the two endpoints selects opposite endpoints.
$$(m_{\rm high}+m_{\rm low})(m_{\rm high}-m_{\rm low}+1)=0,\qquad m_{\rm high}=-m_{\rm low}=j.$$
The endpoint separation counts an integer number of lowering steps, which yields the allowed integer and half-integer labels.
$$2j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\qquad \lambda=j(j+1).$$
For scalar orbital states single-valuedness under a full azimuthal turn restricts the orbital labels to integers.
$$-i\partial_\varphi u=mu,\qquad u(\varphi+2\pi)=e^{2\pi i m}u(\varphi)=u(\varphi),\qquad m\in\mathbb Z.$$

title: Spin one-half and the Pauli matrices
summary: In the ordered $S_z$ basis the spin one-half components take the form $S_i=\hbar\sigma_i/2$.
body: In the ordered $S_z$ basis the spin one-half components take the form $S_i=\hbar\sigma_i/2$.
assumptions: Spin one-half representation and the stated ordered phase convention.
proof:
Order the two states from highest to lowest axial weight and choose their relative phase so the nonzero raising coefficient is positive.
$$S_z|+\rangle=\frac{\hbar}{2}|+\rangle,\qquad S_z|-\rangle=-\frac{\hbar}{2}|-\rangle.$$
The ladder norm with $j=1/2$ fixes the single nonzero raising matrix element and adjointness fixes its lowering counterpart.
$$S_+|-\rangle=\hbar|+\rangle,\qquad S_-|+\rangle=\hbar|-\rangle,\qquad S_+|+\rangle=S_-|-\rangle=0.$$
Take the half-sum and the difference divided by $2i$ to recover the two transverse components.
$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

title: Exchange of identical particles
summary: Exchanging two identical particles in three dimensions gives $P_{ij}\Psi=+\Psi$ for bosons and $P_{ij}\Psi=-\Psi$ for fermions.
body:
Exchanging two identical particles in three dimensions gives $P_{ij}\Psi=+\Psi$ for bosons and $P_{ij}\Psi=-\Psi$ for fermions.

In three spatial dimensions the exchange postulate selects one symmetry sector of the tensor product of labelled one-particle Hilbert spaces, including every internal degree of freedom.
$$P_{ij}\Psi=+\Psi\quad\text{(bosons)},\qquad P_{ij}\Psi=-\Psi\quad\text{(fermions)}.$$
Antisymmetrizing a product with two identical one-particle factors gives zero, since the two exchanged terms have equal magnitudes and opposite signs.

title: Fock space and mode occupations
summary: For one-particle space $h$, the bosonic and fermionic Fock spaces are $\mathcal F_B=\bigoplus_{N\ge0}\operatorname{Sym}^N h$ and $\mathcal F_F=\bigoplus_{N\ge0}\bigwedge^N h$.
body:
For one-particle space $h$, the bosonic and fermionic Fock spaces are $\mathcal F_B=\bigoplus_{N\ge0}\operatorname{Sym}^N h$ and $\mathcal F_F=\bigoplus_{N\ge0}\bigwedge^N h$.

$$\mathcal F_B(h)=\bigoplus_{N=0}^\infty\operatorname{Sym}^N h,\qquad \mathcal F_F(h)=\bigoplus_{N=0}^\infty\bigwedge^N h.$$
Each sector carries the inherited inner product and the zero-particle sector is one-dimensional with normalized vacuum $|0\rangle$.
Choose an ordered orthonormal basis of one-particle modes and specify a normalized occupation basis by $\mathbf n=(n_1,n_2,\ldots)$.
$$\sum_i n_i=N,\qquad n_i\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\ \text{for bosons},\qquad n_i\in\{0,1\}\ \text{for fermions}.$$
Creation inserts the chosen mode as the first tensor factor and projects to the appropriate symmetry, while annihilation is the Hilbert-space adjoint.
$$a_i^\dagger\Psi_N=\sqrt{N+1}\,P_{\pm,N+1}(|i\rangle\otimes\Psi_N),\qquad a_i=(a_i^\dagger)^\dagger.$$
Here $P_{\pm,N}$ averages all permutations, weighted by their sign for fermions and by unity for bosons.

relations.basis: fixes the symmetry of each particle sector
supplies the norm and mode basis
defines annihilation as an adjoint

title: Action of creation and annihilation
summary: Bosonic mode operators carry square-root occupation factors, and fermionic mode operators carry the sign $(-1)^{\sum_{j<i}n_j}$ fixed by mode order.
body: Bosonic mode operators carry square-root occupation factors, and fermionic mode operators carry the sign $(-1)^{\sum_{j<i}n_j}$ fixed by mode order.
assumptions: Ordered orthonormal modes with finite particle occupation and the normalized Fock creation convention.
proof:
Apply the symmetry projector to an ordered bosonic product $w_{\mathbf n}$ and count its distinct permutations.
$$\|P_{+,N}w_{\mathbf n}\|^2=\langle w_{\mathbf n}|P_{+,N} w_{\mathbf n}\rangle=\frac{\prod_j n_j!}{N!},\qquad |\mathbf n\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{N!}{\prod_j n_j!}}P_{+,N}w_{\mathbf n}.$$
Full symmetrization after inserting a mode erases the preliminary symmetrization, so the ratio of the two normalization factors fixes the creation amplitude.
$$a_i^\dagger|\mathbf n\rangle=\sqrt{N+1}\sqrt{\frac{N!}{\prod_j n_j!}}\sqrt{\frac{(n_i+1)!\prod_{j\ne i}n_j!}{(N+1)!}}\,|\mathbf n+\mathbf e_i\rangle=\sqrt{n_i+1}\,|\mathbf n+\mathbf e_i\rangle.$$
Taking adjoint matrix elements in this orthonormal basis lowers an occupied bosonic mode, and an empty mode is annihilated.
$$a_i|\mathbf n\rangle=\sqrt{n_i}\,|\mathbf n-\mathbf e_i\rangle\quad(n_i>0),\qquad a_i|\mathbf n\rangle=0\quad(n_i=0).$$
For fermions the distinct-mode permutations are orthogonal, and the normalization factor for an antisymmetrized ordered product is $\sqrt{N!}$.
When an empty mode is inserted at the front, moving it to its increasing mode position crosses every occupied lower-index mode once.
$$s_i(\mathbf n)=(-1)^{\sum_{j<i}n_j},\qquad a_i^\dagger|\mathbf n\rangle=s_i(\mathbf n)|\mathbf n+\mathbf e_i\rangle\quad(n_i=0).$$
A repeated mode has zero antisymmetrization, and removing an occupied mode by the adjoint crosses the same lower modes.
$$a_i^\dagger|\mathbf n\rangle=0\quad(n_i=1),\qquad a_i|\mathbf n\rangle=s_i(\mathbf n)|\mathbf n-\mathbf e_i\rangle\quad(n_i=1),\qquad a_i|\mathbf n\rangle=0\quad(n_i=0).$$

title: Bosonic and fermionic mode algebra
summary: Bosons satisfy $[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}$ and fermions satisfy $\{a_i,a_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}$ on finite-particle states.
body: Bosons satisfy $[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}$ and fermions satisfy $\{a_i,a_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}$ on finite-particle states.
assumptions: Finite occupation vectors and their linear span, which give a common core for bosonic mode products.
proof:
For one bosonic mode the two orderings have squared amplitudes differing by one.
$$a_i a_i^\dagger|\mathbf n\rangle=(n_i+1)|\mathbf n\rangle,\qquad a_i^\dagger a_i|\mathbf n\rangle=n_i|\mathbf n\rangle.$$
Distinct bosonic mode operations change independent occupation entries with identical factors in either order.
$$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}\mathbf 1,\qquad [a_i,a_j]=[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0.$$
For one fermionic mode insertion followed by removal projects onto the empty state and removal followed by insertion projects onto the occupied state.
$$a_i a_i^\dagger|\mathbf n\rangle=(1-n_i)|\mathbf n\rangle,\qquad a_i^\dagger a_i|\mathbf n\rangle=n_i|\mathbf n\rangle,\qquad a_i^2=(a_i^\dagger)^2=0.$$
For distinct fermionic modes, changing the lower index flips the sign factor of the higher index while changing the higher index leaves the lower sign factor fixed.
If a change is forbidden both orderings vanish, and otherwise their amplitudes are opposites.
$$\{a_i,a_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}\mathbf 1,\qquad\{a_i,a_j\}=\{a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger\}=0.$$
Linearity extends the identities from basis vectors to their finite span.

title: Newton’s laws
summary: In an inertial frame $\dot{\mathbf p}_i=\mathbf F_i$; an isolated particle moves uniformly and reciprocal particle forces obey $\mathbf F_{ij}=-\mathbf F_{ji}$.
body:
In an inertial frame $\dot{\mathbf p}_i=\mathbf F_i$; an isolated particle moves uniformly and reciprocal particle forces obey $\mathbf F_{ij}=-\mathbf F_{ji}$.

For constant mass $\mathbf p_i=m_i\mathbf v_i$. Pairwise cancellation applies to mechanical interactions satisfying the third law; field momentum enters the balance of particles coupled to fields.

title: Momentum and energy balance
summary: For constant masses and reciprocal internal forces $\dot{\mathbf P}=\mathbf F_{\rm ext}$; for conservative total forces $d(T+U)/dt=\partial_tU$.
body:
For constant masses and reciprocal internal forces $\dot{\mathbf P}=\mathbf F_{\rm ext}$; for conservative total forces $d(T+U)/dt=\partial_tU$.

Here $\mathbf P=\sum_i\mathbf p_i$ and $T=\tfrac12\sum_i m_i|\mathbf v_i|^2$.
proof:
Sum the particle equations, pairing the two internal forces for each pair of particles.
$$\dot{\mathbf P}=\sum_i\mathbf F_i^{\rm ext}+\sum_{i<j}(\mathbf F_{ij}+\mathbf F_{ji})=\mathbf F_{\rm ext}.$$
For the energy identity, take the scalar product of each equation with its velocity and sum.
$$\dot T=\sum_i m_i\mathbf a_i\cdot\mathbf v_i=\sum_i\mathbf F_i\cdot\mathbf v_i=-\sum_i\nabla_iU\cdot\mathbf v_i.$$
The total derivative of the potential converts the last sum into the energy balance.
$$\frac{dU}{dt}=\partial_tU+\sum_i\nabla_iU\cdot\mathbf v_i,\qquad\frac{d}{dt}(T+U)=\partial_tU.$$
Zero total external force conserves momentum. A time-independent potential conserves mechanical energy.

title: Virtual work
summary: For ideal constraints $\sum_i(\mathbf F_i-m_i\mathbf a_i)\cdot\delta\mathbf r_i=0$ for every admissible instantaneous displacement.
body:
For ideal constraints $\sum_i(\mathbf F_i-m_i\mathbf a_i)\cdot\delta\mathbf r_i=0$ for every admissible instantaneous displacement.

The applied forces exclude the constraint reactions. Ideality means the reactions do zero total work on each displacement tangent to the constraint surface at fixed time.
proof:
Split the total force into applied force and reaction.
$$m_i\mathbf a_i=\mathbf F_i+\mathbf R_i.$$
Contract each equation with its admissible virtual displacement. Ideality removes the sum of reaction terms.
$$\sum_i(\mathbf F_i-m_i\mathbf a_i)\cdot\delta\mathbf r_i=-\sum_i\mathbf R_i\cdot\delta\mathbf r_i=0.$$
At equilibrium all accelerations vanish and the applied virtual work is zero.

relations.basis: includes the reactions in the equation of motion

title: Mechanical Lagrangian
summary: For a natural mechanical system with a velocity-independent potential, $L(q,\dot q,t)=T-U$.
body:
For a natural mechanical system with a velocity-independent potential, $L(q,\dot q,t)=T-U$.

In holonomic coordinates $\mathbf r_i(q,t)$, $\mathbf v_i=\sum_a\partial_a\mathbf r_i\,\dot q_a+\partial_t\mathbf r_i$ and $T=\tfrac12\sum_i m_i|\mathbf v_i|^2$.

title: Euler–Lagrange equations
summary: For ideal holonomic constraints and potential forces, $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_a}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_a}$ in each independent coordinate.
body:
For ideal holonomic constraints and potential forces, $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_a}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_a}$ in each independent coordinate.

Use regular, independent generalized coordinates and constant masses. All derivatives of the position charts below are evaluated on the trajectory.
proof:
At a fixed time the coordinate variations span the admissible displacements. Substitute them into virtual work.
$$\delta\mathbf r_i=\sum_a\partial_a\mathbf r_i\,\delta q_a,\qquad 0=\sum_a\left[\sum_i(\mathbf F_i-m_i\mathbf a_i)\cdot\partial_a\mathbf r_i\right]\delta q_a.$$
Independent variations force each coefficient to vanish. The potential gives the generalized force by the chain rule.
$$\sum_i m_i\mathbf a_i\cdot\partial_a\mathbf r_i=\sum_i\mathbf F_i\cdot\partial_a\mathbf r_i=-\partial_aU.$$
Differentiate the velocity formula with velocities and coordinates treated as independent arguments.
$$\partial_{\dot q_a}\mathbf v_i=\partial_a\mathbf r_i,\qquad \partial_a\mathbf v_i=\sum_b\partial_a\partial_b\mathbf r_i\,\dot q_b+\partial_a\partial_t\mathbf r_i=\frac{d}{dt}\partial_a\mathbf r_i.$$
Differentiate the generalized kinetic momentum in time. Its second term equals the coordinate derivative of kinetic energy.
$$\frac{d}{dt}\partial_{\dot q_a}T=\sum_i m_i\mathbf a_i\cdot\partial_a\mathbf r_i+\sum_i m_i\mathbf v_i\cdot\partial_a\mathbf v_i=-\partial_aU+\partial_a T.$$
The potential is independent of velocity. Substituting the Lagrangian yields the equation.
$$\frac{d}{dt}\partial_{\dot q_a}L-\partial_a L=0.$$

title: Stationary action
summary: For fixed endpoints and independent smooth variations, $\delta S=0$ for all variations iff $d(\partial_{\dot q_a}L)/dt=\partial_a L$.
body:
For fixed endpoints and independent smooth variations, $\delta S=0$ for all variations iff $d(\partial_{\dot q_a}L)/dt=\partial_a L$.

A stationary trajectory is a path whose first variation vanishes. Stationarity alone does not imply a minimum.
assumptions: Sufficient regularity for differentiating the integrand and integrating the momentum derivative by parts; independent variations with fixed endpoints.
proof:
Vary the path with a fixed test displacement and differentiate under the integral.
$$\delta S=\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}S[q+\epsilon\eta]\right|_{0}=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\sum_a(\partial_aL\,\eta_a+\partial_{\dot q_a}L\,\dot\eta_a)\,dt.$$
Integrate the derivative of the variation by parts; both endpoint variations vanish.
$$\delta S=\left[\sum_a\partial_{\dot q_a}L\,\eta_a\right]_{t_1}^{t_2}+\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\sum_a\left(\partial_aL-\frac{d}{dt}\partial_{\dot q_a}L\right)\eta_a\,dt.$$
Vary one coordinate at a time using compactly supported test functions. The fundamental lemma sets each continuous coefficient to zero.
$$\partial_a L-\frac{d}{dt}\partial_{\dot q_a}L=0.$$
Conversely these equations annul the bulk integrand, and the endpoint conditions annul the boundary term.

title: Hamilton’s equations
summary: For a regular Lagrangian, $H=\sum_a p_a\dot q_a-L$, $\dot q_a=\partial_{p_a}H$ and $\dot p_a=-\partial_{q_a}H$.
body:
For a regular Lagrangian, $H=\sum_a p_a\dot q_a-L$, $\dot q_a=\partial_{p_a}H$ and $\dot p_a=-\partial_{q_a}H$.

Define $p_a=\partial_{\dot q_a}L$ and solve locally for $\dot q(q,p,t)$.
proof:
The nonsingular velocity Hessian is the Jacobian of the momentum map at fixed position and time.
$$\det(\partial_{\dot q_b}p_a)=\det(\partial_{\dot q_b}\partial_{\dot q_a}L)\ne0.$$
Use the inverse velocities in the differential of the Legendre transform.
$$dH=\sum_a(\dot q_a\,dp_a+p_a\,d\dot q_a)-\sum_a(\partial_aL\,dq_a+\partial_{\dot q_a}L\,d\dot q_a)-\partial_tL\,dt.$$
The coefficients of the velocity differentials cancel. Along a solution substitute the Euler–Lagrange equations.
$$dH=\sum_a(\dot q_a\,dp_a-\dot p_a\,dq_a)-\partial_t L\,dt.$$
Comparison in the independent coordinates gives both canonical equations and the explicit time derivative.
$$\partial_{p_a}H=\dot q_a,\qquad\partial_{q_a}H=-\dot p_a,\qquad\partial_t H=-\partial_tL.$$

title: Lorentz group
summary: The Lorentz group is $O(1,3)=\{\Lambda\in\mathbb R^{4\times4}:\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta\}$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$.
body:
The Lorentz group is $O(1,3)=\{\Lambda\in\mathbb R^{4\times4}:\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta\}$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$.

It acts on $X=(ct,x,y,z)^{\mathsf T}$. The proper orthochronous component has $\det\Lambda=1$ and $\Lambda^0{}_0\ge1$.
proof:
Preservation of the interval for every displacement is preservation of its symmetric quadratic form.
$$X^{\mathsf T}\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda X=X^{\mathsf T}\eta X\quad(\forall X)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta.$$
The identity preserves the form; products preserve it by substitution. Rearranging the same equation gives the inverse.
$$(AB)^{\mathsf T}\eta(AB)=B^{\mathsf T}\eta B=\eta,\qquad\Lambda^{-1}=\eta\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta.$$

title: Lorentz boost
summary: For a standard boost along $x$, $x'=\gamma(x-vt)$ and $t'=\gamma(t-vx/c^2)$ with $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$.
body:
For a standard boost along $x$, $x'=\gamma(x-vt)$ and $t'=\gamma(t-vx/c^2)$ with $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$.

Take coincident origins, aligned axes, positive spatial orientation and $|v|<c$. The transverse coordinates are unchanged.
proof:
The moving origin and linearity fix the spatial row. Write the time row with unknown coefficients.
$$\beta=v/c,\qquad x'=a(x-\beta ct),\qquad ct'=bct+dx.$$
Insert the two light rays. Their directions are preserved in a standard boost.
$$x=ct:\ b+d=a(1-\beta),\qquad x=-ct:\ b-d=a(1+\beta).$$
Adding and subtracting gives the time row. Invariance of the interval then determines its scale.
$$b=a,\qquad d=-a\beta,\qquad (ct')^2-(x')^2=a^2(1-\beta^2)[(ct)^2-x^2].$$
Future orientation selects the positive square root.
$$a=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2},\qquad ct'=\gamma(ct-\beta x),\qquad x'=\gamma(x-vt).$$

title: Time dilation
summary: Two ticks of one inertial clock satisfy $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$ in a frame where the clock moves at speed $v$.
body:
Two ticks of one inertial clock satisfy $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$ in a frame where the clock moves at speed $v$.

Proper time is the time interval in the rest frame of the clock.
proof:
The clock has one rest-frame position at the two ticks. The separation in the laboratory therefore follows the clock worldline.
$$\Delta x'=0,\qquad\Delta x=v\Delta t.$$
Insert this displacement into the time transformation.
$$\Delta\tau=\Delta t'=\gamma(\Delta t-v\Delta x/c^2)=\gamma(1-v^2/c^2)\Delta t=\Delta t/\gamma.$$

title: Length contraction
summary: A rod of rest length $L_0$ moving longitudinally at constant speed has simultaneous laboratory length $L=L_0/\gamma$.
body:
A rod of rest length $L_0$ moving longitudinally at constant speed has simultaneous laboratory length $L=L_0/\gamma$.

The rod is at rest in its own inertial frame; both laboratory endpoints are sampled at one laboratory time.
proof:
Choose simultaneous laboratory events at the two endpoints and transform their separation.
$$\Delta t=0,\qquad L=\Delta x,\qquad \Delta x'=\gamma(\Delta x-v\Delta t)=\gamma L.$$
The transformed events need not be simultaneous, but the endpoints have fixed positions in the rest frame. Their spatial separation is therefore the rest length.
$$\Delta x'=L_0,\qquad L=L_0/\gamma.$$

title: Longitudinal Doppler shift
summary: For collinear propagation, a clock moving at $v$ samples $\nu'=\gamma(1\mp\beta)\nu$ for light traveling along or against its velocity.

A clock samples the phase of a monochromatic plane wave on its worldline; one cycle corresponds to a $2\pi$ phase change.
proof:

$$\phi_\pm(t)=2\pi
u_\pm(t\mp x(t)/c),\qquad x(t)=vt.$$

$$
u'_\pm= rac{1}{2\pi} rac{d\phi_\pm}{dt} rac{dt}{d	au}=\gamma(1\mp eta)
u_\pm.$$
For two beams tuned to two rest-frame resonances, multiply the corresponding shifts.
$$ rac{
u_+
u_-}{
u'_+
u'_-}= rac1{\gamma^2(1- eta^2)}=1.$$

title: Trapped electron magnetic moment
body:
For one trapped electron, $-\mu/\mu_B=g/2=1.001\,159\,652\,180\,59(13)$.

Electron in a magnetic field in a Penning trap; compare the electron, not a bound atomic moment.

observation.observable: Magnitude of electron spin magnetic moment in Bohr magnetons
observation.conditions: Electron in a magnetic field in a Penning trap; compare the electron, not a bound atomic moment.
observation.reduction: Extract moment ratio from anomaly and cyclotron frequency measurements with trap corrections.

relations.basis: measures the spin magnetic moment in Bohr magnetons to determine half the free-electron g factor

title: Relativistic lithium ion clock
summary: At $\beta=0.338$, the lithium ion frequency combination was $\epsilon=(1.5\pm2.3)\times10^{-9}$.
body:
At $\beta=0.338$, the lithium ion frequency combination was $\epsilon=(1.5\pm2.3)\times10^{-9}$.

Co- and counter-propagating lasers address two transitions of stored lithium ions at $v/c=0.338$.

observation.conditions: Co- and counter-propagating lasers address two transitions of stored lithium ions at $v/c=0.338$.
observation.reduction: Normalize the product of laboratory resonance frequencies by the product of rest frequencies. The special-relativistic longitudinal Doppler factors cancel in this product.

relations.basis: tests relativistic clock rate together with longitudinal Doppler kinematics
predicts the measured product of the two resonance frequencies
